metadata.title: The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Option (Call/Put, American/European)
nodes.statement: An option is a security giving the right to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at the exercise price $c$. An American option may be exercised any time up to expiration $t^*$; a European option only at $t^*$.
nodes.statement_clean: Definitions of call/put options and American vs European exercise styles.

nodes.name: Option Value Function
nodes.statement: Let $w(x,t)$ denote the value of the option as a function of the underlying stock price $x$ and time $t$. Subscripts denote partial derivatives: $w_1 = \partial w/\partial x$, $w_2 = \partial w/\partial t$, $w_{11} = \partial^2 w/\partial x^2$.

nodes.name: Hedged Position
nodes.statement: A hedged position consists of one share of stock long and $1/w_1(x,t)$ options short, so that to first order its value is independent of small changes in the stock price.

nodes.name: Variance Rate
nodes.statement: The variance rate $v^2$ of the return on a security is the limit, as the measurement interval shrinks, of the variance of the return over that interval divided by the interval length.

nodes.name: Elasticity of Option Price
nodes.statement: The elasticity of the option price with respect to the stock price is $xw_1/w$, the ratio of percentage change in option price to percentage change in stock price.

nodes.name: Ideal Market Conditions
nodes.statement: (a) Constant short-term interest rate $r$; (b) stock price follows a continuous-time random walk with variance rate proportional to $x^2$, hence end-of-interval prices are log-normal with constant variance rate $v^2$; (c) stock pays no dividends; (d) European exercise only; (e) no transaction costs; (f) borrowing at $r$ allowed; (g) no short-selling penalties.
nodes.statement_clean: Seven idealized market conditions under which the valuation formula is derived.

nodes.name: Hedge Ratio
nodes.statement: Number of options to short against one share of stock long: $1/w_1(x,t)$.

nodes.name: Ito Expansion of $\Delta w$
nodes.statement: $\Delta w = w_1 \Delta x + \tfrac{1}{2} w_{11} v^2 x^2 \Delta t + w_2 \Delta t.$
nodes.notes: Stochastic calculus expansion (Ito's lemma applied informally) of the option value.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes Differential Equation
nodes.statement: Under the ideal conditions, the option value $w(x,t)$ satisfies $w_2 = rw - rxw_1 - \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 x^2 w_{11}$, with terminal boundary $w(x,t^*) = \max(x-c, 0)$.
assumptions: $w(x,t)$ is the value of a European call with strike $c$ and maturity $t^*$
conclusions: Boundary condition $w(x,t^*) = x - c$ for $x \ge c$, $0$ otherwise (eq. 8)

nodes.name: Derivation of the Black-Scholes PDE via Riskless Hedge
nodes.statement: Form a continuously rebalanced hedged position; show its return is certain and so must equal $r\Delta t$; equating to the equity yields the PDE.

nodes.name: Form hedged position
nodes.statement: Take one share long and $1/w_1$ options short; equity is $x - w/w_1$ and change over $\Delta t$ is $\Delta x - \Delta w/w_1$.

nodes.name: Apply stochastic calculus to $\Delta w$
nodes.statement: Substituting $\Delta w = w_1 \Delta x + \tfrac{1}{2} w_{11} v^2 x^2 \Delta t + w_2 \Delta t$ gives change in equity $-(\tfrac{1}{2} w_{11} v^2 x^2 + w_2) \Delta t / w_1$.

nodes.name: No-arbitrage: hedge return equals $r\Delta t$
nodes.statement: The hedge return is certain, so it must equal $r\Delta t$ times the equity, otherwise arbitrage; equate $-(\tfrac{1}{2} w_{11} v^2 x^2 + w_2)\Delta t/w_1 = (x - w/w_1) r\Delta t$.

nodes.name: Rearrange to PDE
nodes.statement: Drop $\Delta t$ and rearrange to obtain $w_2 = rw - rxw_1 - \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 x^2 w_{11}$.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes Call Option Formula
nodes.statement: The unique solution of the Black-Scholes PDE with boundary $w(x,t^*) = \max(x-c,0)$ is $w(x,t) = x N(d_1) - c e^{r(t-t^*)} N(d_2)$, where $d_1 = (\ln(x/c) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2)(t^*-t))/(v\sqrt{t^*-t})$ and $d_2 = d_1 - v\sqrt{t^*-t}$.
assumptions: European call with strike $c$, maturity $t^*$, current stock price $x$, current time $t$
conclusions: Option value depends only on $x, t^*-t, c, r, v^2$, not on the stock's expected return

nodes.name: Solution via Heat Equation Reduction
nodes.statement: Substitute $w(x,t) = e^{r(t-t^*)} y[(2/v^2)(r-\tfrac{1}{2} v^2)[\ln(x/c) - (r-\tfrac{1}{2} v^2)(t-t^*)],\, -(2/v^2)(r-\tfrac{1}{2} v^2)^2 (t-t^*)]$ to reduce the PDE to the heat equation $y_2 = y_{11}$, then apply Churchill (1963).

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement: Apply the substitution in eq. (9) reducing the BS PDE to the heat equation $y_2 = y_{11}$ (eq. 10).

nodes.name: Transform boundary condition
nodes.statement: The terminal condition becomes $y(u,0) = 0$ for $u<0$ and $y(u,0) = c[e^{u(\tfrac{1}{2} v^2)/(r - \tfrac{1}{2} v^2)} - 1]$ for $u \ge 0$ (eq. 11).

nodes.name: Apply heat-equation solution
nodes.statement: Use the standard Gaussian-kernel solution of the heat equation (Churchill 1963, p. 155) to write $y(u,s)$ as the Gaussian convolution integral (eq. 12).

nodes.name: Back-substitute and simplify
nodes.statement: Substitute eq. (12) into eq. (9) and simplify to obtain $w(x,t) = xN(d_1) - c e^{r(t-t^*)} N(d_2)$ with $d_1, d_2$ as in eq. (13).

nodes.name: Hedge Ratio Equals $N(d_1)$
nodes.statement: Differentiating the option formula, $w_1(x,t) = N(d_1)$, with $d_1$ as in eq. (13). Thus $xw_1/w > 1$ and the option is always more volatile than the stock.

nodes.name: Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)
nodes.statement: In market equilibrium, the expected return on any asset is a linear function of its $\beta$, defined as the covariance of the asset's return with the market return divided by the variance of the market return.

nodes.name: Alternative Derivation via CAPM
nodes.statement: Apply CAPM to express expected returns on stock and option in terms of $a = E[\text{market return}] - r$; expand $\Delta w$ via stochastic calculus; the $a$ and $\beta_x$ terms cancel, yielding the same PDE (eq. 21 = eq. 7).

nodes.name: Express option's $\beta$ in terms of stock's $\beta$
nodes.statement: From the relation $\mathrm{cov}(\Delta w/w, \Delta m) = (xw_1/w) \mathrm{cov}(\Delta x/x, \Delta m)$ obtain $\beta_w = (xw_1/w) \beta_x$ (eq. 15).

nodes.name: Apply CAPM to stock and option
nodes.statement: Write $E(\Delta x/x) = r\Delta t + a\beta_x \Delta t$ and $E(\Delta w/w) = r\Delta t + a\beta_w \Delta t$; multiply the second by $w$ and substitute eq. (15) to get $E(\Delta w) = rw\Delta t + axw_1 \beta_x \Delta t$ (eq. 18).

nodes.name: Take expectation of stochastic expansion
nodes.statement: Take $E[\cdot]$ of $\Delta w = w_1\Delta x + \tfrac{1}{2} w_{11} v^2 x^2 \Delta t + w_2 \Delta t$ (eq. 19) and substitute $E(\Delta x) = rx\Delta t + ax\beta_x \Delta t$ to obtain $E(\Delta w) = rxw_1 \Delta t + axw_1 \beta_x \Delta t + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 x^2 w_{11} \Delta t + w_2 \Delta t$ (eq. 20).

nodes.name: Cancel $a$ and $\beta_x$ terms
nodes.statement: Equate eq. (18) and eq. (20); the terms involving $a$ and $\beta_x$ cancel, leaving $w_2 = rw - rxw_1 - \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 x^2 w_{11}$ (eq. 21).

nodes.name: American Call on Non-Dividend Stock Equals European Call
nodes.statement: When the stock pays no dividends, an American call is never optimally exercised before maturity, so its value coincides with the European call value given by eq. (13).
conclusions: American call value equals European call value $w(x,t)$ from eq. (13)
nodes.notes: Attributed in the paper to Merton (1973).

nodes.name: European Put Option Formula (Put-Call Parity)
nodes.statement: The European put $u(x,t)$ satisfies the same PDE with boundary $u(x,t^*) = \max(c-x,0)$. Using $w(x,t) - u(x,t) = x - c e^{r(t-t^*)}$, $u(x,t) = -xN(-d_1) + c e^{r(t-t^*)} N(-d_2)$.
conclusions: Put-call parity: $w(x,t) - u(x,t) = x - c e^{r(t-t^*)}$ (eq. 25)
nodes.notes: Put-call parity attributed in the paper's footnote to Stoll (1969).

nodes.name: Independence of Expected Return on Stock
nodes.statement: Eq. (13) does not contain the expected return on the stock; the option's value depends on the stock price but not on the stock's expected return.

nodes.name: Maturity Enters Only via $r(t^*-t)$ and $v^2(t^*-t)$
nodes.statement: $t^*-t$ appears only multiplied by $r$ or $v^2$; an increase in maturity has the same effect as an equal percentage increase in both $r$ and $v^2$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of Option Value
nodes.statement: Merton (1973) showed $w$ as given by eq. (13) is monotonically increasing in each of $t^*$, $r$, and $v^2$, approaching the stock price as a maximum.

nodes.name: Hedged Position with Slope $1/2$
nodes.statement: Stock at \$15, option at \$5, slope $w_1 = 1/2$: hold one share long and two options short, equity \$5. If the stock moves $\pm$\$5, the equity becomes \$4.25 in either direction (a \$0.75 decline due to the second-order $w_{11}$ term).

nodes.name: European Call Pricing Problem
nodes.statement: Determine the no-arbitrage value $w(x,t)$ of a European call option with strike $c$ and maturity $t^*$ on a non-dividend stock with current price $x$ and log-normal price dynamics with variance rate $v^2$, given a constant interest rate $r$.

nodes.name: Warrant Valuation
nodes.statement: Value a corporate warrant accounting for: long maturity (so $v^2$ may change), no dividend adjustment, stepwise exercise prices, mergers, payment of exercise price with bonds at face value, and dilution upon exercise.

nodes.name: Common Stock and Bond Valuation as Options
nodes.statement: Value the common stock and pure-discount bonds of a levered firm by viewing the common stock as a European call on the firm's assets with strike equal to the bonds' face value $c$ and maturity equal to the bond maturity.

nodes.name: Equity as an Option on the Firm
nodes.statement: For a firm with pure discount bonds of face value $c$ maturing in $T$ years, the value of common stock is $w(x,t)$ with $x$ the total firm value and $v^2$ the variance rate of the return on the firm; the bond value is $x - w(x,t)$.
assumptions: Firm has only common stock and pure discount bonds outstanding
Bonds prohibit dividends until paid off
At maturity firm liquidates and pays bondholders before stockholders

nodes.name: Common Stock as Compound Option on Coupon Bonds
nodes.statement: If the firm has coupon bonds, the common stock is a compound option: at each interest payment date the stockholders hold an option to buy the next-period option by making the interest payment. The stockholders' claim equals the value of option $n+1$, where $n$ is the number of remaining interest payments.

nodes.name: Modigliani-Miller Capital-Structure Irrelevance
nodes.statement: Modigliani and Miller (1958) showed that, absent taxes and other imperfections, total firm value is unaffected by capital structure.

nodes.name: Empirical Test Findings
nodes.statement: Empirical tests on a large body of call-option data (Black and Scholes 1972) show option buyers pay prices systematically higher than formula values; option writers receive prices near formula values; the gap is larger for low-risk stocks, suggesting the market underestimates the effect of variance differences.

nodes.name: American Put Option Formula
nodes.statement: No closed-form formula is known for an American put option; an American put is worth strictly more than a European put because early exercise can be optimal when the stock price is near zero.

nodes.name: Adequate Dividend Adjustment for American Calls
nodes.statement: If the stock pays dividends, no exercise-price adjustment is fully adequate to protect the call holder; in extreme cases (a holding company paying out all assets) the option value drops to zero regardless of any adjustment.
